name: Serbian Empire
info: A medieval Eastern Orthodox empire proclaimed by Stefan Dušan in 1346, which stretched from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth and broke apart after the death of Stefan Uroš V in 1371.

facts.successor: Moravian Serbia and other semi-independent lordships, later Ottoman rule

t: Stefan Dušan was crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks in Skopje on 16 April 1346, a title that claimed the succession of the Byzantine Empire.
Dušan's Code, enacted in 1349 and 1354, had 201 articles based on Roman-Byzantine law and is considered a medieval constitution.
Under Stefan Uroš V the empire fragmented into principalities, and it effectively ended with his death in 1371, the year of the Battle of Maritsa.
dyk: Stefan Dušan did not fight a single field battle to win his empire: he took it by besieging cities.
ev: Dušan attacks the Byzantine Empire and takes Ohrid, Prilep and Kastoria
At Serres Dušan proclaims himself Tsar
In Skopje Dušan is crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks, and the Serbian Archbishopric becomes a Patriarchate
The first assembly at Skopje enacts Dušan's Code
Dušan invades Hum and occupies part of the land disputed with the Bosnian Ban Stephen II Kotromanić
A second assembly at Serres completes Dušan's Code
Dušan dies of an unknown illness and is succeeded by Stefan Uroš V
The Ottomans defeat Vukašin at the Battle of Maritsa; Uroš V dies childless on 4 December

sections.foundation:
The Serbian Empire emerged from the Kingdom of Serbia. Stefan Dušan, son of King Stefan Dečanski (r. 1322–1331), held the title of young king and ruled the province of Zeta, as Serbian heirs traditionally did. With the support of most of the nobility, Archbishop Danilo and generals such as Jovan Oliver Grčinić, he besieged his father at Nerodimlje and forced him to give up the throne; the old king died imprisoned in the fortress of Zvečan.

In 1333 Dušan attacked the Byzantine Empire of Andronikos III Palaiologos with the help of the Byzantine general Syrgian, taking Ohrid, Prilep and Kastoria. By 1345 his state covered half of the Balkans, more than either the Byzantine Empire or the Second Bulgarian Empire. That year at Serres he proclaimed himself Tsar, and on 16 April 1346 in Skopje he was crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks. The ceremony was performed by the newly elevated Serbian Patriarch Joanikije II, the Bulgarian Patriarch Simeon and Nicholas, Archbishop of Ohrid. His son Uroš was crowned King of Serbs and Greeks with nominal rule over the Serbian lands.
sections.socioeconomy:
Dušan gave strict orders against piracy and for the safety of travellers and foreign merchants. Relations with Venice were resumed, and the port of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) became an important point of exchange; Ragusan merchants held trading privileges throughout the realm. Roman roads such as the Via Militaris, the Via Egnatia, the Via de Zenta and the Kopaonik road carried wine, manufactures and luxury goods from the coast and metals, cattle, timber, wool, skins and leather from the interior.

Srebrenica, Rudnik, Trepča, Novo Brdo, Kopaonik, Majdanpek, Brskovo and Samokov were centres for iron, copper, lead, silver and gold. The silver mines provided much of the royal income; they were worked by slave labour and managed by Saxons, a colony of whom worked Novo Brdo. The currency was the dinar, also called perper after the Byzantine hyperpyron, and the imperial tax was one dinar per house a year. Kosovo was the most prosperous and densely populated region. Society had an aristocratic basis: nobles held hereditary estates worked by dependent sebri, peasants owing labour services.
sections.military:
Serbian tactics relied on wedge-shaped attacks of heavy cavalry with horse archers on the flanks. The main strength of the army was its heavily armoured knights, alongside hussars, light cavalry armed mainly with spears and crossbows for scouting, raiding and skirmishing. Many foreign mercenaries served, mostly Germans as cavalry and Spaniards as infantry, and the emperor had a personal guard of German knights. The German nobleman Palman commanded this Alemannic Guard from 1331 and led all the mercenaries.

Dušan seized Thessaly, Albania, Epirus and most of Macedonia from the Byzantines, winning by sieges rather than field battles. In October 1350 he invaded Hum with an army said to number 80,000, against the Bosnian Ban Stephen II Kotromanić, who avoided battle and retreated to the mountains. Serbian armies reached Duvno, Cetina, the Krka and Imotski, and some Bosnian nobles submitted, but most Bosnian fortresses held out. In 1355 Dušan was preparing new campaigns in the south and east when he died. Under his son the empire could not repel the Ottoman Turks, who defeated the Serbs under Vukašin at the Battle of Maritsa in 1371.
sections.governance:
The emperors were Stefan Dušan (1346–1355) and Stefan Uroš V (1355–1371); Vukašin of Serbia was co-ruler with the title of king from 1365, and Prince Marko was designated heir as young king from 1369. The monarch had broad powers but was advised by a permanent council of magnates and prelates, and the court, chancellery and administration were rough copies of those of Constantinople.

Dušan's Code was enacted at Skopje on 21 May 1349 and at Serres in 1354 by assemblies of bishops, nobles and provincial governors. Its 201 articles rested on Roman-Byzantine law and on St. Sava's Nomocanon of 1219; articles 172 and 174, on judicial independence, were taken from the Byzantine Basilika. The Code listed the hierarchy as lands, cities, župas and krajištes, the krajištes being frontier župas, and it replaced the title of župan with the Greek-derived kefalija. Dušan raised the Serbian Archbishopric to the Serbian Patriarchate. Influenced by the clergy, he treated Roman Catholicism with severity: converts to the Latin Church were condemned to the mines and its propagators threatened with death.
sections.impact:
Under Dušan, Serbia was one of the most powerful states in Europe and the most powerful in Southeast Europe, a multi-ethnic and multi-lingual empire from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth. Its imperial title claimed the Byzantine succession, and the Byzantines received it with indignation. The Bulgarian Empire under Ivan Alexander, whose sister Helena married Dušan, appears to have supported the coronation and the creation of the Patriarchate of Peć. Dušan also gave sanctuary to John VI Kantakouzenos, the former Byzantine regent then in revolt, and allied with him.

His severity towards Catholics worried the Papacy, which roused the rivalry of the Catholic Hungarians. Schools and monasteries enjoyed royal favour and became institutions that carried on Serbian traditions, and architecture, frescoes and mosaics of the period, influenced by Italian art, survive as its record. The 1339 map of Angelino Dulcert shows a flag with a red double-headed eagle above Skopje for Dušan's realm. During the centuries of Ottoman rule that followed, the memory of the Serbian Empire became an integral part of Serbian national identity.
sections.decline:
Dušan died suddenly in December 1355 and was succeeded by Stefan Uroš V, called the Weak, an epithet that also described the empire as it slid into feudal anarchy. The holdings of a rapid conquest had not been consolidated, and Uroš could neither repel foreign enemies nor check the independence of his nobles. The empire broke into a conglomeration of principalities, some of which did not even nominally acknowledge him. Meanwhile the Ottoman Turks spread from Asia into Europe, taking Byzantine Thrace and then the other Balkan states.

In 1371 the Ottomans defeated the Serbs under Vukašin at the Battle of Maritsa, where much of the nobility was killed, and made vassals of the southern governors; Uroš died childless on 4 December 1371. With no agreed heir, semi-independent provincial lords ruled. Some successors claimed the imperial title in parts of Serbia until 1402, but the lands in Greece were never recovered. Moravian Serbia under Lazar Hrebeljanović became the strongest successor and fought the Ottomans at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Serbia was annexed by the Ottomans in 1459.

summary: The Serbian Empire was the realm Stefan Dušan built by sieges and crowned in Skopje in 1346, an Orthodox empire from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth governed by Dušan's Code. After his death in 1355 it fragmented under Stefan Uroš V and ended in 1371, the year of the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa.

pointDescs.1346: Dušan is crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks in Skopje, ruling half of the Balkans.
pointDescs.1349: Dušan's Code is enacted at the assembly of Skopje.
pointDescs.1350: Dušan invades Hum with an army said to number 80,000 and occupies part of the disputed land.
pointDescs.1354: The second assembly at Serres completes Dušan's Code.
pointDescs.1355: Dušan prepares new campaigns but dies of an unknown illness in December.
pointDescs.1356: The Serbian garrisons in the Dalmatian cities of Klis and Skradin fall; under Stefan Uroš V the empire begins to fragment.
pointDescs.1365: Vukašin becomes co-ruler with the title of king as provincial lords grow independent.
pointDescs.1371: The Ottomans win the Battle of Maritsa and Uroš V dies childless; the empire effectively ends.

notes: The article is short and has no source list, so references are empty.
The article says Dušan besieged the emperor at Salonica in 1340 and imposed a treaty; this conflicts with its own 1334 account and was left out.
The article says the 1350 Bosnian campaign 'seized Bosnia and Herzegovina' in one place but that most fortresses held out in another; the latter is followed.
